title: The Aragonese Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Aragonés
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.
ai_disclosure: Written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the direction of CaminoPlus. Facts in the guides are listed with their sources; routes, closures and services change, so check local information before you walk.

spans.t: The Camino Aragonés begins on a frontier. At the Somport pass in the Pyrenees, a plain roadside milestone marks the start of the road in Spain, and from there you walk down the valley of the River Aragón to Jaca, across a wide open depression called the Canal de Berdún, past the long blue shape of the Yesa reservoir and over the hills of Navarre, to Puente la Reina, where this road joins the Camino Francés. The CaminoPlus catalog gives its length as ~160 km. It is the Spanish end of the old road from Arles, and a quiet way to Santiago.
The promise of this book is simple.

By the last page you will know whether this short, quiet road is yours, how to cut it into six days, what to carry and what to check, and what happens where it ends: at Puente la Reina the Camino does not stop. It joins the French Way.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, and the chapter on other ways to split them.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your day. Each one says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause, and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way".
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It is written from public sources, named at the end, and not from a walk. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
Every distance here carries a tilde,

, because it is approximate. Published lengths differ between sources, and this book says so where it matters. Where something depends on the season (snow at the pass, the heat of a shadeless day, the line of the path beside the reservoir), it says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say to one another as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way; each stamp is a
sello
. A
cabañera
is a broad droving track made by flocks, and on this road the path often follows one. The
Canal de Berdún
is not a canal but a broad valley, and you will cross it in two days.
Places keep their Spanish names here. In Navarre the signs also carry Basque forms, such as Zangoza for Sangüesa.
Carry water, start early, and be ready to slow down.
Buen Camino.
Where it runs

The road starts at the Somport pass, which Aragon's tourism brochure puts at ~1,640 m (Wikipedia gives ~1,632 m). From there it drops down the valley of the River Aragón to Jaca, and the river stays beside you as far as Sangüesa. Between Jaca and Navarre the road crosses the Canal de Berdún, runs along the south shore of the Yesa reservoir, leaves Aragon at a marker stone beyond Undués de Lerda, and climbs and falls through the hills of Navarre by Sangüesa and Monreal. It ends where it joins the French Way, at Puente la Reina.

How long is it? The catalog says ~160 km. The sources give a range. The Aragonese brochure says that about 858 km to Santiago remain at the pass, and the Navarre tourist board gives ~56 km from Sangüesa to Puente la Reina. Stage tables add up to ~164 km. The Confraternity of St James writes ~170 km for the Spanish part of the Arles road, and a Spanish Wikipedia table of distances to Santiago (870 at Somport, 692 at Puente la Reina) implies ~178 km along the route it lists, which takes in the detours by Santa Cruz de la Serós and Lumbier. Take ~160 to ~170 km as the honest range.
One road, several names

Pilgrims call it the Camino Aragonés. The Aragonese government's pages do not: they call it the Camino Francés as it passes through Aragon, and Aragon's tourism brochure adds that many people call it the Aragonese Way. Navarre calls it the second branch of the Camino Francés. In France the same road is the Via Tolosana, the Chemin d'Arles, waymarked as the GR 653. In Spain the Confraternity says it is waymarked with yellow arrows and also with red and white bars as the GR 65.3. The Camino de Santiago entered UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1993, and the Aragonese government takes the route of that inscription as the reference for its stretch of the road.
Why the road is here
Somport is the old
Summus Portus

, the Latin "highest pass". The twelfth-century pilgrims' guide in the Codex Calixtinus describes four roads that start in France and, according to Wikipedia, converge at Puente la Reina. The Confraternity says that the southern one, from Arles by Toulouse, is among them. Pilgrims on it crossed here and not at Roncesvalles, and Wikipedia says that Somport was arguably the most popular Pyrenean pass for pilgrims until the Roncesvalles road became safer in the twelfth century. Aragon's brochure adds that the first crossing into Aragon used a Roman road over the Palo pass and down the Echo valley, and that the Somport route was promoted later.

A hospital at the pass looked after them. The Navarre tourist board's leaflet says the hospital of Santa Cristina was founded in the eleventh century and is already mentioned in the Codex, and Spanish Wikipedia adds that the Codex ranks it among the three great hospitals of Christendom, with Jerusalem and the Great St Bernard pass. Today it is a ruin you walk past in the first hour.

The kings of Aragon shaped the rest. Jaca, Aragon's brochure says, was the first city of the Camino, the capital of the kingdom and the seat of its bishops, and Wikipedia says it was the first capital until 1096. The cathedral was begun in the second half of the eleventh century on the initiative of King Sancho Ramírez, says the Navarre leaflet. The monastery of San Juan de la Peña, off the road above Jaca, became their royal pantheon.
What it feels like

It is a road of changing landscape in six days. At the start you are in a narrow, steep valley of white limestone peaks and dark conifers. The Aragonese government's planning study describes the valley opening out near Villanúa, with Mediterranean crops and warmer air appearing after Jaca. Then comes the Canal de Berdún, which the Confraternity describes as broad arable farmland anticipating the meseta, with rocky "moonscapes" and the huge reservoir. In Navarre the land turns to wheat, vines, pinewoods and wind turbines, and a day of hills brings you down to Eunate and the bridge.

The twentieth century is on this road too. The great international station at Canfranc opened in 1928, and the rail link with France ended in 1970. A road tunnel opened under the pass in 2003. The Yesa reservoir, built around 1960, drowned farmland and emptied villages, and you will walk through one of them.

It is also a road with few walkers on it. Spanish Wikipedia says that few pilgrims use it and, citing the Pilgrim's Office, reports that 404 of the pilgrims who received a Compostela in 2018 began at Somport and 116 at Jaca. The Confraternity says the road has relatively few pilgrims, though their number is growing.
How hard is it?

The CaminoPlus catalog rates the Camino Aragonés 3, the same as the French Way and the Winter Way. A Spanish consumer foundation's stage guide rates each of the six days "medium". Neither tells you where it bites, so here it is.

items.t: Day 1 is long and goes downhill.
It is ~31 km, with a drop of about 800 m from the pass to Jaca. Fit walkers finish it, and their knees remember it.
The middle is exposed.
On the day to Ruesta, that guide says, only the last four kilometres give shade. The Confraternity of St James calls summer on the Arles road too hot.
There are long gaps between villages.

On the way to Ruesta the only place to eat that the guide lists is Artieda, and on the way to Monreal it finds no village between Rocaforte and Izco for ~15 km. The Aragonese government's planning study calls the stretch after Puente la Reina de Jaca more remote, with fewer services. The app's own route notes agree that services are sparse in places.
Some of it runs beside a main road.
Between Somport and Berdún the path keeps close to the N-330 and the N-240, and the Aragonese study describes its many crossings.
The last day starts hard.
Navarre's brochure warns that the first kilometres out of Monreal are demanding.

spans.t: No day is rated above medium. What the road asks for is steady walking, a full bottle and a plan for lunch.
Who it suits

items.t: Someone with a week.
Six days is a common plan, seven is possible, and the road is short enough to walk in one go.
Someone who wants quiet.
Few pilgrims use it, and the Confraternity calls the Arles road solitary but rewarding.
Someone who comes from France.
This is the Spanish end of the road from Arles.
Someone who means to reach Santiago by the French Way
but would rather begin in the high Pyrenees than at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. The roads join at Puente la Reina, and the Camino goes on from there.
Someone who likes old stones.
On or near the road are a ruined pilgrims' hospital, the cathedral at Jaca, Romanesque churches at Santa Cruz de la Serós, Sangüesa and Eunate, and an abandoned village.
A self-sufficient walker.
You will carry water and food, follow a map, and be comfortable with silence.

spans.t: Who might choose another road

items.t: If you want company,
the French Way is the most popular of all the routes, according to Wikipedia, and you will meet many more people there.
If you want the Compostela from this walk alone,
this is not the road. The chapter on arriving explains why, and sends you to the Pilgrim's Office.
If you walk slowly and need short days,
the chapter on other ways to split the road offers a seven-day plan, but there are only a few places to stop.
If you plan to walk in winter,
the Confraternity advises against crossing the pass in snow or mist, unless you are an experienced mountain walker.
If you dislike walking beside traffic,
you will meet the N-330 and N-240 more than you may like.

spans.t: How it compares

In general terms, the French Way is longer and busier, and this road is shorter and quieter. It starts higher and ends by feeding into the other. Leaving Obanos, just before Puente la Reina, the consumer foundation's guide notes a line of pilgrims much longer than usual. You will feel the change.
The short answer

The Confraternity of St James says the Arles road, of which this is the Spanish end, can be walked all year, and that spring (long daylight, flowers) and autumn are best. It calls summer too hot, and it advises against winter journeys over the Somport pass in snow or mist, except for experienced mountain walkers.

The CaminoPlus app's route notes put the best months at May to September. The two views differ, and the difference is worth knowing. May and September fall within both. July and August are where they part.
What the weather does

This book has climate figures for one place only, Jaca, near the top of the road. Wikipedia gives figures from the World Meteorological Organization and describes a submediterranean climate with cool winters, warm summers, common frost, snow common from late November to early March, and the rainiest seasons in autumn and spring.

items.t: January:
daytime highs of about 10 °C, and lows around −1 °C.
April and May:
highs of about 16 °C and about 21 °C.
July:
highs of about 29 °C, with lows of about 14 °C.
October:
highs of about 19 °C, and lows of about 7 °C.
Rain:
about 770 mm a year, with no real dry season.

spans.t: These are Jaca's figures, at ~820 m. The pass is much higher, so expect it to be colder. Aragon's planning study notes that temperatures keep rising as the valley opens out below Jaca. The Confraternity warns that Aragón can be chilly and windy even in summer, and that the Somport is snow-covered in winter.
Daylight

A standard solar calculation for Jaca gives about 9 hours of daylight in late December, about 12 hours in mid-March and mid-September, and about 15 hours at midsummer, when the sun rises around 06:25 and sets around 21:40 on summer time. In mid-October it sets at about 19:20. If you walk in autumn or winter, plan to arrive before dark.
A season at a time

items.t: Spring.
Long days, green hills and cool mornings. Snow may still lie at the pass early in the season, so ask before you set off. The Confraternity's pick.
Summer.
On a day that the stage guide calls shadeless, the sun is the main thing you walk against. Start at first light, rest in the middle of the day, and carry more water than seems sensible.
Autumn.
Shorter days and more rain, but milder air. The Confraternity's other pick.
Winter.
Short days and snow at the pass. The Confraternity does not advise the crossing, and this book agrees.

spans.t: Crowds

Few pilgrims walk this road. Spanish Wikipedia, citing the Pilgrim's Office, counts 404 pilgrims who received a Compostela in 2018 after starting at Somport. You may often have the path to yourself. You will meet far more people once you join the French Way.
Check before you go

items.t: Snow and mist at the pass.
Ask in Jaca or Canfranc, and check the forecast, before you set off from Somport.
Heat.
In summer, look at the forecast for the Canal de Berdún before the two long days.
Opening seasons.
Some small albergues and the campsites keep only a season. One stage guide gives March to October for volunteer hosts in one village. Ask ahead.
The reservoir.
The Aragonese government's 2018 planning study says that works to enlarge the Yesa reservoir would affect two stretches of the path near Artieda and Ruesta. Ask locally which line is open.

spans.t: The credencial
The
credencial

is the pilgrim's passport. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago describes the official model as a cardboard card of sixteen concertina-folded pages. It says you can ask for one in person at the Office or at institutions the cathedral authorises: parish churches, associations of Friends of the Way of St James, pilgrim hostels, confraternities and others. It also describes a digital credential, an app for Android and iOS.

The Office says the credencial gives you no rights as such, and names two practical uses: access to the hostels offered by the Christian hospitality of the Way, and proof when you apply for the Compostela. Stamps, the
sellos

, are normally collected where you sleep, but also in parish churches, monasteries, town halls and other places. Get your credencial before you leave home, or at a place that issues it, and do not assume you can buy one at the pass.
Getting there

Somport is a frontier pass in the mountains, and you will probably spend the night before in Canfranc or Jaca. Public transport changes, so this book gives no times. The Confraternity of St James mentions train and bus services over the Pyrenees between Oloron-Sainte-Marie and Jaca, and Wikipedia says the station at Canfranc has been served by trains from Zaragoza. Check what runs now, and ask in Jaca or Canfranc about the last stretch up to the pass.
Plan to arrive the day before, so that you can start Day 1 early. It is one of the two longest days of the road.
Getting home

If you finish at Puente la Reina and go on along the French Way, you need no plan. If you stop there, Pamplona is ~24 km back along the French Way. The Navarre tourist board lists a bus line from Pamplona to Sangüesa, which helps if you stop at Sangüesa instead. Do not plan a tight connection for the day you finish.
Training

You will walk six days of ~22 to ~31 km, and the first day is almost all downhill. Walk with your loaded pack for a few weeks beforehand, on as many hills as you can find, and practise descents, which punish the knees more than climbs. Break in your shoes. If you have a health worry, ask your doctor before you book.
What to pack
Navarre's tourism pages say the lighter your luggage the better, and that is the first rule.

items.t: Layers for a cold start.
You begin at ~1,640 m, where the morning can be cold even in summer. Pack a warm layer, a waterproof, a hat and gloves.
Sun and water.
A wide hat, sun cream and bottles that hold about two litres between them. The shadeless days are long.
Food for the gaps.
The chapters on the days say where the villages are far apart.
A head torch,
for dark rooms and early starts.
Poles,
if you use them, for the long descent of Day 1.

spans.t: Shoes and feet
A Spanish consumer foundation's stage guide warns that the broad droving tracks, the
cabañeras

, of the second day can wear the soles of the feet and bring on sore tendons, especially in heavy, high boots. It recommends light trail shoes. Whatever you choose, walk in them before you start, carry blister dressings, and treat a hot spot the moment you feel it.
Money

Take cash. Aragon's tourism brochure, a 2009 print, advises drawing money in Jaca because cash machines are scarce until Sangüesa, and some small places may not take cards, so ask. Carry some small notes and coins.
Language and signs
Spanish will do everywhere. In Navarre the official signs also carry Basque forms: Sangüesa is also Zangoza, Monreal is also Elo, and Puente la Reina is also Gares.

The road is waymarked with the yellow arrow and, as the GR 65.3, with red and white bars. The stage guide says that in Aragon wooden posts mark the path, and that in Navarre these give way to stone markers with a shell and a yellow arrow. The Aragonese planning study found in 2018 that some stretches, for example the northern line by Berdún beyond Puente la Reina de Jaca, had no signs at all. Keep a map saved on your phone, because signal can fail in the valleys.
Health
If you fall ill, the Navarre tourism pages point to the European Health Insurance Card for visitors who may need care. Check what your own cover includes. In an emergency, call

chapters.title: Down from the pass: Somport to Jaca

spans.t: How the days are counted

Stage counts and lengths vary by source. The day lengths in this book are rounded from a Spanish consumer foundation's stage guide, which cuts the road into six days from Somport. They were checked against Navarre's own brochure for the two Navarre days, and against Aragon's tourism brochure for the villages and the distance to the border. Other guides differ by a kilometre or two, and where they differ by more the book says so. The six days add up to ~164 km, and the catalog says ~160 km. The guide's practical notes, such as where to eat, are several years old, so treat them as a question for the app and for the people you meet.
The character of this day

One long day takes you from the top of the road to its first city. You start at ~1,640 m, at a frontier pass of ski slopes and old customs buildings, and finish in Jaca at ~820 m, after a drop of about 800 m in ~31 km. The Aragonese government's planning study, which describes this stretch section by section, calls the valley V-shaped, cut deep by the river, with pale limestone peaks above dark conifers. The V opens into a U near Villanúa, the hills soften, and by Jaca there are fields.
Day 1: Somport to Jaca (~31 km)

At the pass, Aragon's brochure says, a plain monolith at the roadside announces the Camino through Aragon, and the path starts on the left of the N-330. The brochure puts about 858 km between you and Compostela. Steps lead down beside the river. Within about 800 m, a stage guide says, you pass the excavated ruins of the hospital of Santa Cristina. Navarre's leaflet says it was founded in the eleventh century and is mentioned in the Codex Calixtinus. It is a pile of stones now, but stop for a minute. Spanish Wikipedia says that pilgrims who had climbed the pass, often tired, hungry and ill, found rest at the hospital, and that the Codex says they were given lodging for three days.

Below it the path passes Candanchú, crosses the N-330 several times around the Rioseta ravine, and runs among the old concrete bunkers built to defend the frontier. The Aragonese study says the path crosses the road three times at the bends of the ravine. Take each crossing slowly. At ~7 km you reach Canfranc Estación. Its great international station opened in 1928, and trains stopped running to France in 1970. Just beyond the village the path passes the mouth of the road tunnel that opened in 2003, and the brochure asks pilgrims to take great care there and for the next ~500 m.

Canfranc itself comes at ~11 km, a long single street with a medieval bridge. Villanúa is at ~16 km, where the valley widens. The Aragonese study says that the holm-oak woods near it are the most northerly in Europe. After Villanúa the path follows the river or droving tracks beside the road to Castiello de Jaca, at ~23 km.

The last ~8 km follow the river and the edge of the N-330 to the hermitage of San Cristóbal, ~28 km from the pass. After that comes a steep little climb into Jaca. The stage guide estimates the whole day at 8 hours 30 minutes.

If it is too much, the day can be cut at Canfranc or Villanúa, and the places are named above. If you can, start early, take the descent gently, and keep an eye on the weather over the pass. The Confraternity of St James says Somport is snow-covered in winter.
Jaca

Jaca deserves an evening and, if you can spare it, a day. Aragon's brochure calls it the first city of the Camino, the capital of the kingdom of Aragon and the seat of its bishops. Wikipedia says it was the first capital until 1096. The cathedral was begun in the second half of the eleventh century on the initiative of King Sancho Ramírez. The citadel, a perfect pentagon with moat and bastions, was ordered by Philip II in about 1592. The brochure says you can walk the perimeter along the glacis.
Aragon's brochure advises drawing cash here, and the Aragonese study finds fewer services beyond Puente la Reina de Jaca, so Jaca is the place to stock up.

chapters.title: The Canal de Berdún: Jaca to Ruesta

spans.t: The character of these days

Two days take you across a wide, open valley that the river has cut through grey marl and sandstone. Flat-topped hills carry the villages, wheat fills the terraces, and the white peaks of the Pyrenees stay on the northern horizon. Peña Oroel, which Aragon's brochure puts at ~1,770 m, stays behind you for a long time. The Confraternity of St James describes the Canal de Berdún as broad arable farmland anticipating the meseta, with dramatic rocky "moonscapes".

After Puente la Reina de Jaca the Aragonese government's planning study finds the least altered landscape of the Aragonese road, with a calm rhythm over the wide valley and no road noise. It also calls the stretch more remote, with fewer services, and the stage guide lists few places to stop. Carry what you need for each day, as the chapter on sleeping and eating explains.
Day 2: Jaca to Arrés (~25 km)
The way leaves Jaca beside the N-240 and keeps close to it for most of the day. A stage guide says it follows broad droving tracks, the
cabañeras

, along the verge, and it warns that they are hard on the feet and that you must cross the main road in several places with great care. Santa Cilia comes at ~15 km, a village laid out in a neat grid, and the guide calls it the official intermediate stop of the day. From there the path runs beside the N-240 again to Puente la Reina de Jaca, at ~21 km.

This is not the Puente la Reina where you will finish. It is a small village in Huesca, named for its stone bridge over the Aragón, and the two are ~110 km apart. In 2018 the Aragonese study found the main road here very hard for a walker to cross, with no pedestrian-crossing signs, so cross with care. Pilgrims have built little towers of pebbles on the river bank here, and Aragon's brochure admires them.

Then comes the climb: ~3 km, of which the first is the hardest, on a path up the flank of the mountain to Arrés, which stands at ~700 m on a rocky crest. Aragon's brochure says it was a royal town and that the ruins of its castle look out over the Canal de Berdún. It is a good place to end the day.
Detours.

Two famous places lie off this road above Jaca. Santa Cruz de la Serós is ~4 km up a side road from the N-240, and has a Romanesque church of Santa María, which Navarre's leaflet calls the only remnant of the royal women's monastery that King Ramiro I founded. San Juan de la Peña, above it, is the old monastery built under a great rock, with a Romanesque cloister and the burial place of the early kings of Aragon, according to Aragon's brochure, which puts it ~22 km from Jaca. The Aragonese study says a branch of the GR 65.3 climbs there by Atarés and returns by Santa Cruz. The stage guide calls the climb from the road terribly demanding, and says the visit can also be made by taxi. On foot by the monastery, it counts ~29 km from Jaca to Santa Cilia, against ~15 km direct.
Day 3: Arrés to Ruesta (~29 km)

This is a long day, ~29 km, and the stage guide says that only its last four kilometres have shade. Start at first light. The path leaves Arrés on a stony track through box bushes, then follows farm tracks across the plain, past grey eroded gullies the guide calls badlands, and crosses two ravines on walkways.

Mianos is a village on a hill to one side. Artieda, at ~18 km, stands on a hilltop at ~650 m, and the guide lists it as the only place to eat on the day, so leave Arrés with food and water. It is also the end of a shorter day: the guide suggests ~18 km as an easier alternative. Beyond Artieda, ~11 km remain with no village. The way follows the A-1601 for a while, climbs through an oak wood that offers the first real shade, and passes the ruined Romanesque chapel of San Juan before coming down to Ruesta.

Ruesta is the village the reservoir emptied. The guide says the waters of the Aragón, Esca and Regal were dammed in 1959 and flooded ~2,400 hectares, and that three villages were abandoned. Wikipedia says it was inaugurated in 1960, so sources differ by a year. Aragon's brochure says that in 1988 the Ebro water authority gave Ruesta over to be brought back to life, and it describes a ruined castle with two slender towers. It is a quiet place, and a strange one to walk through.
The reservoir and the path.

The Aragonese study of 2018 says that two stretches of the road here, ~2.8 km before Ruesta and ~500 m after it, would be affected by works to enlarge the Yesa reservoir, and that the Ebro water authority proposed a new line.
Check before you go
which line is open, and ask where you sleep.

chapters.title: Into Navarre: Ruesta to Puente la Reina

spans.t: The character of these days

Three days take you out of Aragon and across the hills of Navarre to the meeting of the roads. The first is a climb over a ridge above the reservoir and a descent to Sangüesa. The second crosses high farmland between two valleys, with few villages. The third is the longest, with a hard start. The Navarre tourist board describes the country as undulating, rich in grain, with windmills, wide pinewoods and wild gorges. It gives ~56 km from Sangüesa to Puente la Reina.
Day 4: Ruesta to Sangüesa (~22 km)

Leaving Ruesta, the path crosses the Regal on a wooden walkway and passes a Romanesque hermitage of Santiago, abandoned, says the stage guide. Then it climbs for ~5 km on a forest track to a high point, with a view over the reservoir, the abandoned village of Tiermas and the ridge of Leyre. The guide warns of a sharp left turn, ~3 km from Ruesta, that is easy to miss.

Undués de Lerda, at ~11 km, is the last village in Aragon. Beyond it the path leaves the village and runs down a ridge. Aragon's brochure says a large marker stone shows the boundary between Aragon and Navarre, and the guide says that the signs change there: the wooden posts of Aragon give way to stone markers with a shell and a yellow arrow. From Undués to Sangüesa the brochure counts ~11.5 km, and the guide counts ~10.5 km, so the sources differ by a kilometre. The guide advises carrying enough water, above all in summer.

Navarre says the road enters its territory at Sangüesa. Its church of Santa María la Real, which Navarre calls an example of the passage from Romanesque to Gothic, has a doorway that the tourist board calls one of the high points of Spanish Romanesque art. Give it time. The old nucleus of Sangüesa is Rocaforte, across the river, says the guide, and King Sancho Ramírez gave it the charter of Jaca in the late eleventh century. The same law tied the two towns together.
Day 5: Sangüesa to Monreal (~27 km)

There are two ways to Monreal, and Navarre's brochure describes both. The main way goes by Rocaforte and the Alto de Aibar. The brochure calls it harder but almost without tarmac, and the stage guide gives it ~27 km. It climbs, and the guide puts the highest point at ~770 m. The distances marked on the brochure's profile add up to ~25 km, so the figures vary by a couple of kilometres.

The climb out of Sangüesa to Rocaforte is steep, and the brochure says to carry water. The way crosses grain, vines and olives, passes under a wind farm, and reaches the Alto de Aibar. The brochure says that a dozen kilometres of valleys and pines lie between there and the next village, Izco, and the guide counts ~15 km with no village between Rocaforte and Izco and only a couple of springs. Carry food and water for the whole of it.

The second way goes by Liédena and the Foz de Lumbier, a gorge that a greenway follows along the old Irati railway. The guide calls it ~5 km longer, but gentler and through villages, and Navarre's brochure offers it to anyone who cannot face Rocaforte. Navarre's page describes the gorge as a natural reserve.

After Izco the path goes to Abínzano and Salinas de Ibargoiti, then through an oak wood to Monreal, at ~555 m. Navarre's brochure calls it a former hunting residence of the kings of Navarre, and says a Gothic bridge leads you in.
Day 6: Monreal to Puente la Reina (~31 km)

Navarre's brochure says this day can be hard because of the ups and downs of the first kilometres, and the guide counts ~13 km of continual ups and downs on the slopes of the Alaiz range as far as Tiebas. There are fountains at Yárnoz, Otano and Guerendiáin. Tiebas has a ruined castle of the thirteenth century, once a home of the kings of Navarre.

After Tiebas the path follows the edge of the motorway and passes under it, through Muruarte de Reta and Olcoz, and past Enériz. Eunate comes at ~26 km. The octagonal Romanesque chapel stands alone in the fields, ringed by a portico of 33 arches. Navarre dates it to the second half of the twelfth century and says its Templar origins feed many legends. The guide says its purpose is still uncertain, and that scholars have suggested both a Templar work and a funeral chapel.

A kilometre or so after Eunate the path climbs to Obanos. There, in the Plaza de los Fueros, says the guide, pilgrims from Roncesvalles and pilgrims from Somport come together. Puente la Reina lies ~3 km further on. The chapter on arriving explains the question of where exactly the roads meet.

chapters.title: Other ways to split the road

spans.t: Six days, seven days

This book follows six days, the plan of the consumer foundation's stage guide. Aragon's own tourism brochure divides its part of the road into four stages: Somport to Jaca, Jaca to Arrés, Arrés to Artieda, and Artieda to Undués de Lerda. Add Undués to Sangüesa, which the brochure counts at ~11.5 km, and the two Navarre days, and you have seven. The CaminoPlus website's list of routes gives 6 to 7 stages, its own editorial range. Both plans work.
The seven-day plan, with lengths rounded from the same guide, looks like this:

items.t: Somport to Jaca (~31 km).
Jaca to Arrés (~25 km).
Arrés to Artieda (~18 km).
Artieda to Undués de Lerda (~22 km).
Undués de Lerda to Sangüesa (~11 km).
Sangüesa to Monreal (~27 km).
Monreal to Puente la Reina (~31 km).

spans.t: The sums come to ~165 km. Days 3 to 5 are shorter. They also split the long day from Arrés to Ruesta, so that you do not carry a whole day's food across the shadeless plain.
You can also cut Day 2 at Santa Cilia, ~15 km from Jaca, and Day 1 at Canfranc or Villanúa. The road has few villages, so ask ahead before you shorten a day.
The northern line

After Puente la Reina de Jaca the Aragonese government's study shows two lines. The southern one, by Arrés, Mianos and Artieda, is the one in this book. The northern one runs beside the N-240 by Berdún, Sigüés, Escó and Tiermas, and Spanish Wikipedia's table takes it on by Yesa and Javier to Sangüesa. The Aragonese study found it unsigned along much of its length in 2018, and says that part of its old line lies under the reservoir. The study calls the southern line the main one, and so does this book.
Detours

items.t: Santa Cruz de la Serós and San Juan de la Peña.
See the chapter on Jaca to Ruesta. It adds about 14 km: the stage guide counts ~29 km from Jaca to Santa Cilia by the monastery, against ~15 km direct.
The Foz de Lumbier.
The second way from Sangüesa to Monreal, ~5 km longer.
Leyre.

Navarre's tourism page puts the monastery ~12 km from Sangüesa. It is a Romanesque monastery with an eleventh-century crypt and a lavishly decorated doorway, and Navarre's brochure says that pilgrims on foot do not pass it. Navarre's page also mentions Gregorian chant.
Javier.
The castle, birthplace of St Francis Xavier, patron of Navarre, lies ~8.5 km off the Camino from Sangüesa, and the page says thousands of Navarrese come in March on the
Javieradas
, a pilgrimage in his honour.

spans.t: Decide about Leyre and Javier before you leave Sangüesa, not after.
Where to rest

Jaca is the obvious place for a rest day, at the end of the long first day and before the quiet middle. Sangüesa is the other. Navarre's page says its streets hold palaces, churches and convents, and the stage guide calls it the second-largest town on the road after Jaca.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office names access to "hostels offered by the Christian hospitality of the Way" as the first use of the credencial, and says that hostels without subsidies are kept going by what pilgrims contribute. Leave a place cleaner than you found it, and give what you can.

The Confraternity of St James says it is now possible to walk almost the whole Arles road using only pilgrim accommodation, gîtes in France and albergues in Spain. On this road the places are small and few, and their seasons vary. A stage guide says that in one village volunteer hosts usually run the albergue from March to October, and that the communal dinner there is paid for by donations. Ask before you rely on a bed, and call ahead on the days with few villages.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and pack your rucksack in the hall in the morning.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed.
Earplugs are a small comfort that goes a long way. If you are the one who snores, apologise at breakfast.
Keep your valuables close.

spans.t: Bedbugs

can be a risk in any shared bed. Check the seams of the mattress, keep your pack and clothes off the bed, and if you find bites, tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. It is a reason to look before you lie down, not a reason to avoid hostels.
If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. It is not cheating.
Eating
Many places on a Camino offer a
menú del peregrino

, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask what is on it, and what it costs, before you sit down. On this road the villages are small, and a bar or shop may be closed when you arrive, so do not leave the evening meal to chance.
Food and water in the gaps

This is the part of the road that needs planning. The stage guide lists Artieda as the only place to eat on the day from Arrés to Ruesta, and it counts ~15 km with no village, and only a couple of springs, on the way from Rocaforte to Izco. The Aragonese study says the stretch after Puente la Reina de Jaca has fewer services, and Aragon's brochure advises drawing cash in Jaca.

items.t: Fill your bottles at the last village,
and carry more than you think you need on a shadeless day.
Carry lunch,
and something for the evening on the two sparse days.
Ask the evening before.
A small village's bar or shop may be shut when you pass, so ask your host what to expect on the next day.
Do not drink from a stream or trough
unless you know it is meant for people.

spans.t: Resting
A day of rest is part of the walk. This road offers two natural places for one.

items.t: Jaca,
after the long first day. See the chapter on Somport to Jaca.
Sangüesa,
before the long hills of Navarre.

spans.t: Listen to your body before you listen to your plan. If something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, stop and rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.
This chapter is plain on purpose. Nothing in it is a reason to stay at home. It is what a careful walker does on a road with a mountain start and long gaps.
Feet and legs

Your feet decide how the walk goes. Stop at the first hot spot and dress it. Change your socks at lunch if they are damp, rest for a few minutes each hour, and eat and drink before you are hungry or thirsty.

Day 1 is a descent of about 800 m in ~31 km. Shorten your stride, use poles if you have them, and rest your knees at Canfranc or Villanúa if they complain. A stage guide says the hard droving tracks of the second day can wear the soles and bring on sore tendons. If you feel a sharp or growing pain in a knee, shin or foot, stop. A day lost to rest is better than a week lost to an injury.
Mountain weather

The pass is where mountain weather matters most. The Confraternity of St James says the Somport is snow-covered in winter, that winter journeys over it in snow or mist are not advised except for experienced mountain walkers, and that Aragón can be chilly and windy even in summer.

items.t: Look at the forecast the evening before and again in the morning.
AEMET, the Spanish state weather service, publishes forecasts. Look at the high ground, not only the town you are leaving.
Start early,
so that a slow morning does not leave you on the mountain at dusk.
Wet clothes cool you quickly.
Carry a waterproof, a warm layer and a hat, and keep one dry layer in a bag.
In mist, stay on the marked way.
If you cannot see the next marker, stop, and go back to the last one you saw.
If the day looks wrong,
change the plan. Wait in Canfranc, or stay a night in Jaca.

spans.t: Heat and shade

The Confraternity calls summer on the Arles road too hot, and the stage guide says that on the day from Arrés to Ruesta only the last four kilometres have shade. On a hot day, start at first light, wear a hat, put on sun cream, drink often and rest in the middle of the day. A headache, dizziness or nausea in the heat are signs to stop, get into the shade, and drink. If they do not pass, ask for help. In dry summers, ask locally about closed paths and fires.
Roads

Much of the first two days runs beside trunk roads. The Aragonese study shows the path crossing the N-330 several times near Canfranc, and Aragon's brochure asks pilgrims to take great care at the mouth of the road tunnel, and for the next ~500 m beyond it. The study found the main road at Puente la Reina de Jaca very hard for walkers to cross in 2018, and the stage guide says to cross the N-240 with the greatest caution.

The Policía Foral de Navarra, in its 2026 advice leaflet for pilgrims, says that on roads you should walk on the left, facing the traffic, using the shoulder if there is one. Keep to a single file in a group. At night or in poor light, use lights or reflective gear. Better still, do not walk on a road in the dark or in thick mist.
The reservoir
The Aragonese study of 2018 says that works to enlarge the Yesa reservoir would affect two stretches of the path near Artieda and Ruesta, and that the Ebro water authority proposed a new line.
Check before you go
, and ask where you sleep.
Water and food

The gaps between villages are the main practical risk of this road: the day from Arrés to Ruesta, and the way from Rocaforte to Izco. Leave with full bottles and food for the whole stretch, and tell your host where you are going.
Staying safe on your own

Tell someone where you plan to sleep each night, and message them when you arrive. Keep your phone charged, carry your map saved on it, and know the name of the last village you passed. Signal can fail in the valleys.
When to stop

Stop, and get help, for chest pain, a fever, severe dizziness, a fall with a blow to the head, a swollen joint, or anything that frightens you. Stop too if you are cold and cannot warm up, if you are lost in mist, or if you have run out of water. A doctor is the right person for a worry, and a plan can always change. The Way will still be there.
Emergencies
is the European emergency number and it works in Spain. Say where you are as exactly as you can: the village, the day, the last landmark you passed.
Every reason is a reason

People walk the Camino Aragonés for faith, for sport, for grief, for curiosity, for a rest from work, or for no reason they can name yet. This book does not rank them. The Pilgrim's Office describes the credencial as meant for those who walk with a Christian sentiment, "even if it is only with an attitude of search". You are welcome on the road whatever you bring to it, and the road does not ask you to explain.
A road of beginnings

This road begins at a frontier, on a high pass, with a ruined hospital a few minutes below it. The Codex Calixtinus, says Spanish Wikipedia, ranks that hospital among the three great hospitals of Christendom, a place where tired pilgrims who had climbed the pass were taken in. You walk down past the stones where they rested, and the whole first day is a long descent.

You may find that this changes the walking. A climb makes you earn each hour, and a descent may leave the head clear while the knees do the work. Later, on the open plain of the Canal de Berdún, there is little to look at but sky and field. A road with few walkers on it leaves plenty of room for whatever comes up.
Ruins and returns

Ruesta is an empty village that has been partly brought back, and Navarre's leaflet says the Romanesque hermitage of Santiago near it was begun at the start of the eleventh century. The reservoir took the fields that fed these villages. Aragon's brochure says that when the water falls at the end of summer, the ruins of the drowned village rise out of it. You do not have to make anything of this. But a road that passes places lost and places remade may suit someone who is also in the middle of something.
Where the roads meet

At the end, the road joins another. A stage guide says that in Obanos pilgrims from Roncesvalles and pilgrims from Somport come together, and it describes a pilgrim-shaped monument on the way in to Puente la Reina inscribed, in translation: "And from here all the Ways to Santiago become one." After several quiet days you will walk into the company of a great many people. Some may find it a gift and some a shock. Either is allowed. You can keep walking alone among them.

If you walk in grief, the road holds you without asking. If you walk with doubt, walk with it. If you walk for sport, walk well, and notice who is walking beside you. If you walk with others, leave a day of the road to yourself.
Questions for the walk
Take one a day, and let it ride in your pocket. You do not have to answer.

items.t: What are you carrying that you could put down?
What did you come here to leave behind, and what did you come to find?
What would you do with this hour if you were not in a hurry?
Who do you wish were walking beside you, and what would you say to them?
What in your life has been emptied out, and what could be returned to it?
When did you last feel that you had enough?

spans.t: A companion for the road
The Library has a small book made to go with this road,
Songs for the Climb
: eight days with the Psalms of Ascent, a morning reading and an evening reflection for each. You can read it before you go, on the road or at home.
When the road is hard

Some days the descent is only a descent and the plain is only a plain. On those days the kindest thing is a short plan: the next village, the next marker. Walk to that, and ask for help when you need it.
Where the roads meet

Navarre's tourist board says that the Aragonese road joins the one that enters Spain by Luzaide/Valcarlos at Puente la Reina, and Aragon's brochure agrees. The Confraternity of St James says the roads join at Obanos, just before Puente la Reina, and so does the stage guide, which puts Obanos ~3 km short of the town. Wikipedia's French Way table notes that the Aragonese road joins just before Puente la Reina. The guide adds that there has been much speculation about which of the two it is, and that official signs lead up to Obanos, though some pilgrims turn left onto the NA-6064 road and go straight to Puente la Reina.
For a walker it comes to a few kilometres either way, and it hardly matters. The catalog ends the road at Puente la Reina, and so does this book.
The bridge

Puente la Reina, Gares in Basque, takes its name from its bridge. Navarre's leaflet calls it an eleventh-century Romanesque bridge ~110 m long, with seven round arches, the easternmost buried, and a protected Site of Cultural Interest. Wikipedia counts six arches. The stage guide says it was built for the passage of pilgrims at the order of a queen. Walk across it slowly. After the quiet of the road from Somport, the main street, with its churches, makes a gentle end to the day.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Compostela is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for Christian purposes, and the Office says that in modern times it is limited to those who come for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.
What this means for this walk

From Puente la Reina to Santiago the sources give ~690 to ~700 km. That is far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for. The walk from Somport to Puente la Reina, ~160 km, is not the last hundred kilometres of any road to Santiago, and it does not end at the cathedral. The Camino goes on along the French Way.

The Office's pages read for this book do not mention the Aragonese Way, or list the routes it recognises. So this book does not say what the Office would record for a walk that stops at Puente la Reina, and it does not say whether any other start counts. If you walked the Via Tolosana in France before Somport, the Office's rule of seventy kilometres in Spain is written for pilgrims who walked a recognised route outside Spain, and how it applies to you is a question for the Office. Ask it before you go, in any doubtful case, whether you are stopping here or going on.
Then what?
You have three choices. You can stop, and enjoy having walked a whole road. You can rest a day and walk on along the French Way.
The French Way

, the first book in this series, covers the rest of the road to Santiago. Or you can go home and come back for the rest another year. Pamplona is ~24 km behind you on the French Way, and Estella ~22 km ahead.
Whatever the Compostela means to you, it is a record of a road you walked, not a measure of it.
If you stop here

A short road ends quickly, and the quiet can arrive all at once. Give yourself a day before the journey home. Sit somewhere with a view of the bridge, wash your clothes, and write down what you remember before the details soften: the cold at the pass, the shadeless plain, the ruined village, the first sight of Eunate. If you carry your credencial home, the stamps are a record of where you slept, and they will mean more in a year than they do tonight.
Do not plan a tight connection for the day you finish. From Puente la Reina, Pamplona is ~24 km back along the French Way, and you will want your onward travel sorted before the last stage.
If you go on

The Camino does not end at Puente la Reina. You can carry on at once, along the French Way, with a rest day first if you can spare it. The road you have just walked is a good preparation: you have six days of legs, your feet have told you what they think of your shoes, and you know how much water you need.
Keeping the Way alive

items.t: Walk again.
You can come back another year and pick up at Puente la Reina.
Read the other books in this series,
if you want to know what lies ahead.
The French Way
has the road from here.
Pass it on.
Say
Buen Camino
to the next walker you meet, wherever you are.

spans.t: When the days at home feel ordinary, remember that you carried everything you needed on your back for a week, and that you walked from a mountain pass to the place where the roads become one.
Buen Camino.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. It lists the Camino Aragonés as a route, from Somport to Puente la Reina, ~160 km, but this book makes no claim about what the app holds for it today, so look in the app, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.

A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office describes a paper credencial and a digital credential of its own. This book says nothing about the passport in any other app, and you should ask the Office whether it counts.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Gobierno de Aragón

(aragon.es): the page on the Directriz del Camino de Santiago, Camino Francés a su paso por Aragón, and its planning study (Tomo I), which describes the path section by section from the Somport to the border with Navarre.
Turismo de Aragón
, the regional tourism board: its brochure
El Camino de Santiago por Aragón
(a 2009 print), for the four Aragonese stages and the villages.
The Gobierno de Navarra
, through its tourism site (visitnavarra.es): the page on the French-Aragonese route, the printed
Camino de Santiago
guide (fifth edition, November 2023), the leaflet of milestones (2021), and the advice leaflet of the Policía Foral (2026).
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the rules of the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Chemin d'Arles.
The Fundación Eroski

(caminodesantiago.consumer.es): the six stage pages of the French Way "by Somport", which give the day lengths, the places along each day and the practical warnings. This is a private foundation's guide and not an official source, and the book attributes it each time.
Wikipedia

, for history, geography and climate: the articles on Somport, the Aragonese Way, the French Way, the Way of St. James, Jaca (with its table of World Meteorological Organization figures), the Yesa Reservoir, Canfranc International railway station and Puente la Reina; and the Spanish Wikipedia's articles on the Camino de Santiago Francés en Aragón and on the Hospital de Santa Cristina de Somport.
A standard solar calculation
, for the hours of daylight at Jaca.
The CaminoPlus route catalog
, for the road's start, end, ~160 km and difficulty rating, and the CaminoPlus website's list of routes, for its 6 to 7 stages.

spans.t: Published figures differ between these sources, so every distance in this book is marked ~. Where the sources say nothing, as on the present line of the path beside the reservoir, the book says nothing and tells you to check. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the villages and towns who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Cabañera
: a broad droving track made by flocks.
Canal de Berdún
: the broad valley of the River Aragón between Jaca and Navarre.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
: the waymarked long-distance path of the Camino in Spain, with red and white bars.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Javieradas
: the pilgrimages to the castle of Javier each March.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
Via Tolosana
: the road from Arles by Toulouse, of which this is the Spanish end.
